title: A Positive D Is Not Proof

scenes.tts: Compare a sampled African genome and a sampled Eurasian genome with a Neanderthal genome. The Eurasian genome shares more derived variants with the Neanderthal. At each site, a chimpanzee shows which allele is ancestral, and a derived variant is a newer one. Where does the surplus come from? Two different histories could both explain it.
scenes.visual: Three genome bars (African, Eurasian, Neanderthal) over a chimp reference; match marks pile up between Eurasian and Neanderthal; two question-mark arrows appear.
scenes.narration: Compare a sampled African genome and a sampled Eurasian genome with a Neanderthal genome. The Eurasian genome shares more derived variants with the Neanderthal. At each site, a chimpanzee shows which allele is ancestral, and a derived variant is a newer one. Where does the surplus come from? Two different histories could both explain it.

scenes.tts: Count the sites. At an A B B A site, the Eurasian and the Neanderthal share the new variant. At a B A B A site, the African and the Neanderthal share it. Suppose you count six hundred A B B A sites and four hundred B A B A sites. D is the difference divided by the total, which comes to zero point two.
scenes.caption: Count the sites. At an ABBA site, the Eurasian and the Neanderthal share the new variant. At a BABA site, the African and the Neanderthal share it. Suppose you count 600 ABBA sites and 400 BABA sites. D is the difference divided by the total, which comes to 0.20.
scenes.visual: Two bars, ABBA 600 and BABA 400 (hypothetical), grow; D = (600-400)/(600+400) = 200/1,000 = 0.20 on a scale from -1 to +1.
scenes.narration: Count the sites. At an ABBA site, the Eurasian and the Neanderthal share the new variant. At a BABA site, the African and the Neanderthal share it. Suppose you count 600 ABBA sites and 400 BABA sites. D is the difference divided by the total, which comes to 0.20.

scenes.tts: With no gene flow and one randomly mating ancestor, the model predicts equal counts, so D equals zero, but here the Eurasian genome shares more. But do not read D as twenty percent ancestry. Old structure in a subdivided African population can also make D positive. A positive D is consistent with gene flow. It is not proof.
scenes.caption: With no gene flow and one randomly mating ancestor, the model predicts equal counts, so D = 0. Here the Eurasian genome shares more. But do not read D as 20% ancestry. scenes.visual: Null case in this sketch: equal bars, D = 0. Then the 600/400 bars with D = 0.20. Two panels: gene flow arrow from Neanderthal; old subdivided African population with no arrow. Both give D above 0.
scenes.narration: With no gene flow and one randomly mating ancestor, the model predicts equal counts, so D = 0. Here the Eurasian genome shares more. But do not read D as 20% ancestry. Old structure in a subdivided African population can also make D positive. A positive D is consistent with gene flow. It is not proof.

scenes.tts: Time can separate the two stories. Recombination breaks up DNA that entered from another population as it passes down the generations, so surviving pieces get shorter on average. Gene flow tens of thousands of years ago leaves long blocks, because recombination has had limited time to break them up. Old structure leaves much shorter pieces on average. So segment length carries information about timing.
scenes.visual: A chromosome bar with one long Neanderthal block; over generation steps recombination cuts it into pieces. Then recent flow = long blocks, old structure = short pieces.
scenes.narration: Time can separate the two stories. Recombination breaks up DNA that entered from another population as it passes down the generations, so surviving pieces get shorter on average. Gene flow tens of thousands of years ago leaves long blocks, because recombination has had limited time to break them up. Old structure leaves much shorter pieces on average. So segment length carries information about timing.

scenes.tts: Ust Ishim was a Homo sapiens man from western Siberia, who lived about forty-five thousand years ago. His genome carried Neanderthal segments longer than those in present-day people. Dated genomes should carry longer segments if gene flow happened shortly before they lived, and old structure predicts only a slight change with age. From the lengths, researchers inferred gene flow seven to thirteen thousand years before he lived. That estimate carries the uncertainty of the recombination model.

scenes.tts: Fit both histories as explicit models to the same data and compare them. So the evidence supports Neanderthal gene flow into the ancestors of the sampled non-Africans. Keep the conclusion to those samples, because it says nothing by itself about other contacts. A positive D is a clue. Test it with segment length.
